items.title: Kagi Mail Opens Its Public Beta at $99 a Year, Without End-to-End Encryption
items.summary: Kagi Mail is now open to anyone, and it isn’t end-to-end encrypted. Kagi, the company behind the paid, ad-free Kagi search engine and the Orion browser, announced the public beta on Monday. You can take a @kagimail.com address or bring your own domain, try it free for 60 days and then pay $99 a year or $9 a month, plus sales tax. It comes included with Kagi Ultimate, the $25-a-month top plan. The announcement promises “no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in.” The word “encryption” doesn’t appear in it. The answer is in the FAQ on the product page : your mail is encrypted at rest and in transit, and there’s no end-to-end encryption or PGP, because Kagi Mail “has to read your mail to flag what needs you.” The launch drew more than 120 comments on Hacker News within a few hours, and encryption was one of the early questions there. As we published, the only other coverage came from forums and a few small tech sites.

items.title: Cleverbridge Confirms Attackers Copied Payment Card Data From Its Platform
items.summary: Cleverbridge confirms attackers stole payment card numbers, expiry dates and CVV codes, warning customers to watch for fraudulent transactions. Cleverbridge, which runs checkouts, payments and subscriptions for other companies, has confirmed that attackers copied payment card data from its platform. The company says it found the problem on 4 November and started notifying affected people on 20 November. That’s a gap of 16 days. “On 4 November 2026, Cleverbridge detected unauthorised activity in our platform and took immediate steps to contain the incident.” reads the incident update published by the company. “Whilst our investigation remains ongoing, regretfully, we have been able to determine that a third party copied payment card data stored on our platform.” Affected systems went offline for a short time and were back online the same day. Only later did the investigation show that a third party had copied payment card data stored on the platform, and the company says that the investigation is still running. The company’s website lists customers such as SUSE, Red Hat and Parallels, but the company has not said which businesses were affected. If you bought a product or service from a company that uses Cleverbridge, it may have handled your payment and stored your card details. Cleverbridge provides payment and subscription services to software and SaaS companies. Cleverbridge has not clearly explained what information was stolen on its public incident page. It says the exposed data may include payment card details and directs affected customers to check their individual notifications. However, a notification reviewed by BleepingComputer provides more details: the stolen information may include card numbers, expiration dates and CVV or CVC security codes. That last item is the one that matters. The card industry’s own rules generally bar companies from keeping the security code once a payment is authorised, so BleepingComputer asked Cleverbridge why the codes were accessible at all. The company did not disclose technical details about the attack, however, its answer excluded a ransomware attack. “None of our systems were encrypted.” continues the update. Cleverbridge says it hired TransUnion/Cyberscout, a third-party vendor, to support the notifications, and that a notice sent on its behalf is legitimate. It has offered credit or identity monitoring where available, with sign-up details in the notice. Asked why people weren’t told sooner, it says it moved fast and notified them without undue delay. Cleverbridge advises users to watch for phishing attempts and warns that it will never request card details, passwords or security codes by email, phone or text. “As always, we recommend that our users follow general best online security practices, remain vigilant, and be aware of phishing attempts.” the company states. “Out of an abundance of caution, please be cautious of unexpected emails, calls, or messages about this incident. Cleverbridge will never ask you for your card details, passwords, or security codes by email, phone, or text message. ” Call your card issuer sooner rather than later. Cleverbridge says the issuer may decide to replace your card after you report the incident. We recommend that you check your card statements carefully and tell your card issuer right away about any transaction that you do not recognise.” concludes the report. “You may also wish to contact your card issuer to tell them about this incident and follow any advice they give, as they may decide to replace your card. ” Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, payment card data)

items.title: How SASE Vendors Design their Solution - Part 5: Outage Survival—Does SASE Work When the Platform Dies?
items.summary: The Achilles' Heel of Cloud Services: Platform OutagesThe shift to cloud-delivered security introduces a new category of risk: platform outages. What happens to your organization’s security and connectivity if the SASE vendor's central management platform goes down? For many businesses, the internet is their corporate network, and a SASE outage can mean a complete corporate blackout.This is where one of the most critical architectural differentiators comes into play: the separation of the data plane and the control plane. A well-designed SASE platform is architected for SASE blackout resilience, ensuring that even a catastrophic failure of the central management infrastructure does not bring a customer's network to a halt. The Good: Strict Data Plane and Control Plane SeparationThe "good" design is one that maintains a strict separation between the Data Plane and the Control Plane.The Data Plane consists of the global network of enforcement nodes (POPs) that process and inspect live traffic. Its sole responsibility is to forward packets and apply security policies at line rate.The Control Plane is responsible for all management functions: the admin console, policy configuration, logging, and reporting.In a resilient architecture, the data plane is designed to operate autonomously. Each enforcement node maintains a local cache enforcement copy of the organization's security policies. If the control plane experiences a complete outage—meaning the admin UI is down, logs are not being processed, and policy changes cannot be made—the data plane continues to function without interruption. User traffic continues to flow, and the last known security policy continues to be enforced.This architectural principle of Data Plane Control Plane separation is the cornerstone of disaster recovery for SASE. It ensures that a vendor's management outage does not become their customer's network outage. The Ugly: A Tangled Mess of InterdependenciesIn contrast, many legacy SASE providers have architectures with dangerous interdependencies between their data and control planes. In these systems, the enforcement nodes may need to make real-time queries to the control plane to retrieve policy information, or the logging and data planes may be so tightly coupled that a failure in one can cascade and impact the other.This is the "ugly" design. If the central management or logging infrastructure fails, the data plane nodes can be left in a state of confusion. They may be unable to process new connections, or worse, they may fail-open, allowing traffic to bypass security inspection entirely. In the most severe cases, the entire service can go down, causing a total network outage for all customers.Furthermore, a resilient architecture extends to the endpoint agent. Smart agents should have automated agent failover mechanisms built in. They should be aware of multiple enforcement nodes and be able to automatically select a backup path if their primary node becomes unavailable. They should also have local bypass parameters that can be triggered as a last resort to maintain connectivity.For any organization evaluating a SASE vendor, the question of architectural resilience should be paramount. An outage is inevitable; how the platform survives it is a direct result of its design. A platform built with a strict separation of the data plane and control plane is one that is built for survival.

items.title: Microsoft Entra Connect Health Breach Exposes Tenant Metadata and Admin Details
items.summary: Microsoft Entra Connect Health breach exposed tenant metadata and admin details, potentially enabling targeted phishing and social-engineering attacks. Microsoft has disclosed a data breach involving its Entra Connect Health service, which exposed tenant metadata and administrator contact details. “On 9 November 2026, we detected a vulnerability in the Microsoft Entra Connect Health API that was introduced on 23 July 2026. The vulnerability could allow an unauthorized party to access tenant and service-monitoring metadata and potentially make changes to Connect Health monitoring configuration.” the company wrote on Reddit. Microsoft Entra Connect Health is a cloud service that helps administrators monitor the health, performance and alerts of their on-premises identity systems. The IT giant says no passwords, authentication tokens or valid cryptographic keys were compromised, but the exposed information could still help attackers craft convincing phishing and social-engineering attacks. The issue came from a vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API, introduced on July 23, 2026. Microsoft identified the flaw on November 9 and deployed a server-side fix on November 19. “We deployed and fixed the vulnerability on 19 November 2026. On 20 November 2026, we concluded our investigation and determined that unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata associated with your organization had occurred. We did not identify any unauthorized configuration changes.” the IT giant added. Customers do not need to install a software update because Microsoft addressed the problem on its side. The attackers could only view the data, but the exposure still created risks. They gained access to administrator email addresses, tenant IDs, domain names and synchronisation status. Attackers could use this information to plan targeted attacks and impersonate Microsoft support staff, service providers or internal IT administrators. Microsoft has not disclosed how many tenants were affected. However, several administrators and managed service providers have reported receiving notifications from the company, suggesting that the breach may have affected many customers. Microsoft says no software update or customer remediation is needed because the Entra Connect Health API vulnerability has been fixed. However, it recommends several precautionary steps. Organisations should alert security and IT teams to possible targeted phishing and social-engineering attempts, ensure administrator accounts use phishing-resistant MFA, and apply Privileged Identity Management for just-in-time access. They should also run Microsoft’s read-only PowerShell script to review potentially exposed metadata, check Connect Health settings, and examine Entra audit logs, sign-in logs and Azure Activity Logs for suspicious activity. Microsoft advises verifying the security notice directly through Azure Service Health rather than clicking email links. items.title: Prism Medical Products Data Breach Affects 1.3 Million Individuals
items.summary: North Carolina-based Prism Medical Products, LLC, a home medical supply provider acquired by the global healthcare distributor and solutions provider Henry Schein Inc. in January 2021, has announced a cybersecurity incident involving unauthorized access to patient data. The sensitive data of more than 1.3 million individuals was potentially compromised in the incident. According to its October 30, 2026, data breach notice, the incident was first identified on October 19, 2026, when suspicious activity was observed within certain parts of its network. Assisted by third-party cybersecurity experts, Prism Medical Products confirmed that an unauthorized third party accessed its network, and it appears that files containing patient information were obtained in the incident. Prism Medical Products said it took immediate steps to prevent further unauthorized access, including disabling remote access and changing credentials, and believes that those measures, along with additional security measures it has implemented, have ensured that its IT environment is safe and secure. Prism Medical Products did not state whether ransomware was used in the incident or if it received a ransom demand. A third-party vendor was engaged to review the affected data and confirmed that the data compromised in the incident includes names, addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses in combination with some or all of the following: medical and clinical information, health insurance information, payment and financial account information, and certain identifiers, such as Social Security numbers, driver’s license numbers, and other forms of government identifiers. Notification letters are now being mailed to the affected individuals, who have been offered 24 months of credit monitoring and dark web monitoring services. Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy While not mentioned by Prism Medical Products in its data breach notice, this appears to have been a cyberattack by a ransomware and data theft/extortion group called Wallstreet. The group first appeared in June 2026 and has targeted companies in multiple sectors, including healthcare, insurance, automotive, manufacturing, construction, government, and public sector firms. While the incident is not yet shown on the HHS’ Office for Civil Rights breach portal, the Oregon Attorney General was informed that the data breach affected 1,326,066 individuals.

items.title: Zero-day Flaw in Medical Imaging App Identified and Exploited AI Agents
items.summary: A zero-day vulnerability in an open-source AI-assisted medical imaging tool has been identified and exploited by an autonomous agentic AI platform. A threat actor linked to China is believed to be behind a series of attacks targeting educational institutions in East Asia (excluding mainland China) between September 8 and September 10, 2026. According to Amazon Threat Intelligence, which shared the findings of the investigation, the threat actor used a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI-based penetration testing framework, which was instructed to obtain shell access. Aside from configuring Cairn, the attack is believed to have had minimal human involvement. The AI-based pen testing tool used multiple AI agents to identify and exploit a zero-day vulnerability in the MONAI Label open-source medical imaging tool, which researchers use to speed up dataset annotation. It took 11 minutes to map the application’s API, identify a path traversal vulnerability, and exploit it to write files outside an intended storage directory. In a subsequent session, the agents wrote a Python reverse shell that automatically loads when Python starts and triggered an API endpoint to establish root access to the server. After the zero-day vulnerability was discovered, the threat actor stepped in and provided the agents with a proxy that tunnelled into a second university network, which was running the same vulnerable software. The researchers believe the threat actor used the same zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel, then instructed the agents to attack other devices on the network. Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Amazon Threat Intelligence discovered the campaign as the publicly hosted Carin instance used by the attackers was left exposed on the internet and could be accessed without authentication. Prompts were discovered to have been written in simplified Chinese, with timestamps in the executed scripts configured to China Standard Time. The vulnerability affects MONAI Label versions up to and including 0.8.5. The researchers notified the maintainers of MONAI Label, and the vulnerability will be fixed in version 0.5.6. The security advisory was published on GitHub on November 18, 2026, and contains workarounds for hardening security ahead of the release of the fixed version. The researchers warned that autonomous AI agents are already being used to find and exploit software vulnerabilities, and they can do it faster than security teams can react and triage a security alert. The researchers also describe an attempt by the AI agents to compromise a Redis target. The AI agents ran continuously for 16 hours and kept adapting, performing 148 sequential actions without any human involvement. “To keep pace, organizations should prioritize high-confidence detections that trigger automated response, with humans overseeing outcomes rather than reviewing every individual action,” suggest the researchers.

items.title: CrowdStrike buys missing network security piece in $43.9B Zscaler deal
items.summary: CrowdStrike agreed to acquire cloud security company Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal on Monday, combining endpoint protection with zero-trust network security in one of the largest cybersecurity acquisitions ever and intensifying the industry’s race to build broad security platforms. The deal brings together CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform, which focuses on endpoint, identity and cloud security, with Zscaler’s cloud-delivered network security and zero-trust access capabilities. CrowdStrike said the combined company is expected to begin with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR). The acquisition also addresses a strategic gap in CrowdStrike’s portfolio. While the company has expanded beyond endpoint protection into identity, cloud security and threat intelligence, Zscaler brings an established security service edge (SSE) and zero-trust network access platform. “With Zscaler, CrowdStrike will enter network security, cybersecurity’s largest single addressable market segment,” CrowdStrike said in a statement. items.title: Bulgaria Discovers Massive Government Breach After Five Years of Undetected Spying
items.summary: Bulgaria uncovered a five-year cyberespionage campaign that stole 130GB of government files. The attacker and full impact remain unknown. Bulgaria ‘s ministry for innovation and digital transformation announced it had uncovered a hacking operation running since 2021. Reuters reports that more than 130 GB of documents, about 62 million pages, were downloaded from government databases over those five years. Minister Ivan Vassilev said there’s no evidence so far that Bulgarian citizens’ personal data was compromised. “The minister, Ivan Vassilev, said that since 2021 more than 130 GB, ​or 62 million pages, of documents had ​been downloaded, but that there was no evidence ⁠so far that Bulgarians’ personal data had been compromised, ​Nova TV reported on its website.” Reuters reports . The breach came to light only after Bulgaria introduced a new national cybersecurity monitoring system, which spotted suspicious activity in August. Until then, the country apparently had no system in place capable of detecting an intrusion that had been going on since 2021. This raises questions not only about the attackers’ capabilities but also about the lack of security monitoring inside government networks. Several international hacking groups may be behind the attack, but investigators haven’t linked it to any specific country or nation-state actor. The stolen files reportedly include cabinet documents, reports and communications between ministries and government agencies. “We discovered that several international hacker groups had accessed Bulgarian systems starting in 2021,” Vassilev said. “The information they stole included sensitive details of how Bulgarian state institutions operate” “At this stage, there is no evidence that the personal data of Bulgarian citizens has been affected,” the minister added. After the attack was discovered, several agencies joined the response, including intelligence services, the defense ministry, police, cybersecurity experts and international partners such as the EU’s cybersecurity agency. Authorities have isolated the affected systems, blocked the attackers’ access and removed the malware. Prosecutors have also been informed. Vassilev wants them to investigate not only the hackers but also whether government agencies failed to detect the intrusion earlier. The government also has questions to answer. Bulgaria went through several unstable governments and repeated elections during the five years the attackers remained inside its systems. This political instability may have affected long-term investment in cybersecurity. An attack that went unnoticed from 2021 to 2026 doesn’t only raise questions about the attackers’ skills. It also highlights how weak security monitoring allowed them to stay hidden for so long. This isn’t first time Bulgaria faced a major breach, and the contrast is worth noting. In 2019, hackers stole roughly 11 GB of data from the National Revenue Agency, exposing personal details on nearly five million citizens, about 71% of the population at the time, and a Russian link was floated before a 20-year-old local suspect was arrested. This time the target was institutional correspondence rather than citizen records, and the scale of documents taken, 130 GB against 11 GB, dwarfs that earlier case. What’s missing from Wednesday’s announcement is almost everything that would let the public judge the real damage: who did this, what specific documents went out the door, and whether any of it has already been used. Bulgaria’s own cybersecurity agency, BTA, described the find as “Government Uncovers Apparent Years-Long Breach of Administrative Networks”, language that tells you an investigation is still very much open, not closed. Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, Bulgaria)

items.title: Meta Suspends DeFlock America Facebook Group, Citing Its “Dangerous Organizations” Rule
items.summary: Meta has suspended DeFlock America, the biggest Facebook group organizing against Flock Safety’s license plate cameras. The news came from Facebook user David Eduard, who posted a screenshot of Meta’s notice to the group’s admins on Sunday. Dated 21 November, it says Meta suspended the group because some of the activity on it “may not follow our rules,” and that this goes against its Community Standards on dangerous organizations and individuals. Eduard put the group at more than 840,000 members; IBTimes UK reported 818,000, Facebook’s own count, in late September. “Suspended for thought crimes,” Eduard wrote. By Monday his post had about 1,400 reactions and more than 500 shares, and the story had moved to Hacker News and Lemmy. We found no coverage by larger outlets as we published. When we tried to open the group on Monday while logged in to Facebook, it showed only the generic “This content isn’t available right now” page, which doesn’t give a reason. Meta hasn’t commented yet.

items.title: Clever AI prompt ideas every security leader should steal
items.summary: For all the talk of AI use by attackers and defenders, little attention is paid to ways CISOs and their security pros can leverage AI uniquely to expediate tasks, cut through the noise, facilitate decision-making, and potentially save big on auditing. Several specific AI prompts can help security leaders and staff handle multiple critical tasks not typically associated with AI for cyber defense, such as risk management, compliance, policy development, and critical thinking. Developing truly useful prompts isn’t particularly easy, however, because it often requires a significant amount of research and effort, not to mention lots of fine-tuning, which can take security teams away from other critical tasks. Fortunately, the security community is here to help, with advice on unique prompt ideas that have greatly aided them in strengthening security, facilitating decision-making, and saving time for hands-on defense. Create an adversarial assistant to control damage — and cut down AI slop Dzmitry Romanovadvocates establishing an AI prompt that acts as a second security reviewer to help catch latent problems before any damage occurs. The key, though, is to give it an adversarial twist so that it looks at a situation from the attacker’s perspective while critiquing the human security reviewer’s ideas. “What am I missing? items.title: VirtualBox Process Hardening on Windows 2026 Edition: What’s a Single Bit Between Friends?
items.summary: Back in 2017 I did some research into Oracle VirtualBox on Windows. Specifically I focussed on their mechanism to protect their VM processes from the user on the host. The protection was to gate who could open the kernel driver, which might allow for privilege escalation due to the way it was designed. At the time I found 3 ways of bypassing the protection, with an additional issue in COM’s runtime I reported in 2020. These issues were all written up in this post. Fast forward to 2026 and I decided to look at VirtualBox again to see if much had changed. This time I found 3 new bypasses for protected processes, with an additional bug which was a broken fix for the 2020 bypass breaking due to changes in Windows. In this blog post I want to focus on one specific issue CVE-2026-87268 which abused a feature of the .NET Framework which, when combined with the implementation of the DLL loader hooks implemented by VirtualBox, permitted a bypass of the checks and allowed me to load arbitrary code into the protected process. Let’s dig into the root cause of the issue in .NET first, before moving on to exploitation in VirtualBox. ### .NET Assembly Loading The .NET Framework is interesting when it comes to bypassing process hardening as it supports loading assemblies from a memory buffer as long as you stick to only using managed code. This is obviously useful if the hardened process is maintained through verifying what DLLs can or cannot be loaded as it bypasses the traditional image mapping process. As the .NET runtime implementation is Microsoft signed, it’s usually permitted to load by any such checks. The canonical way to load from a memory buffer is to use the Assembly::Load static method which accepts a byte array. This does require you to run some .NET code first, or find a confused deputy to do the work for you. I used this API method to bypass VirtualBox process hardening back in 2017, I was able to get to the API through the JScript script engine, culminating in me releasing the generic DotNetToJScript tool. I’d always assumed this was the limit of bootstrapping arbitrary .NET from a memory buffer. If you tried to load a .NET assembly from a file it’d map it as an image section which would hit any DLL hardening checks and block an unsigned and untrusted binary from loading. However, in a “Doh” moment I realized I’d never verified this behavior to be true, thus I decided to take a look. The most important function to mapping a .NET assembly into memory seems to be `PEImageLayout::Map`, which is roughly the following in the version 4 of CLR.DLL which implements the runtime: ``` PEImageLayout *PEImageLayout::Map(HANDLE file) { PEImageLayout* image = new MappedImageLayout(file); if (!image->Image) { image = new FlatImageLayout(file); } if (image->Image) { if (!PEDecoder::CheckFormat(image->Image)) ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); } return image; } ``` What is interesting is this code creates a `MappedImageLayout` object based on the file. If that fails it’ll fall back to using a different object, `FlatImageLayout`. The names kind of give away what they’re doing, but just to be sure let’s look at the implementations of the constructors: ``` void MappedImageLayout::MappedImageLayout(HANDLE file) { HANDLE mapping = CreateFileMapping(file, nullptr, SEC_IMAGE | PAGE_READONLY); if (mapping) { this->Image = CLRMapViewOfFileEx(mapping); } else { if (GetLastError() != ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT) ThrowLastError(); } DWORD policy = 0; if (EEConfig::EnforceCodeIntegrity() || (SUCCEEDED(WldpGetLockdownPolicy(nullptr, &policy, nullptr)) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_OFF(policy) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_CONFIG_CI(policy)) ) { ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); } // ... } ``` The constructor for `MappedImageLayout` uses the CreateFileMapping API to convert the file handle into a section object. The code passes the `SEC_IMAGE` flag which instructs the kernel to assume the file is a PE executable and build an image section object including mapping in executable memory pages. Any protections which rely on verifying an image’s signature or location can be notified and take appropriate action. However if the `CreateFileMapping` call fails the code checks if the last error was not `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT` and throws ending the load entirely. An additional check is made here to check if “Code Integrity” is enforced through the Windows Lockdown Policy (WLDP) APIs. This checks for the “Dynamic Code Security” code integrity policy being enabled or if a User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI) policy is enforced. If it is then an error is thrown ending the loading process. We’ll come back to this check when it becomes relevant. Assuming the mapping fails with the `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT` error, then the loading process continues, creating a `FlatImageLayout` object instead: ``` void FlatImageLayout::FlatImageLayout(HANDLE file) { HANDLE mapping = CreateFileMapping(file, nullptr, PAGE_READONLY); if (mapping) { this->Image = CLRMapViewOfFileEx(mapping); } else { ThrowLastError(); } // ... } ``` This constructor is simpler, it just calls `CreateFileMapping` without the `SEC_IMAGE` flag. Therefore the file is mapped into memory as a data only section. There’s no executable pages, but that doesn’t matter for .NET. The final check, back in the first code snippet verifies that the PE file is valid with a call to `PEDecoder::CheckFormat`, throwing if it’s not valid. The take away from this is if we can get .NET to load a valid assembly file, but cause the first call to `CreateFileMapping` to fail with the `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT` error we can get it to execute the file from memory. Any protection code which is expecting to check the loaded image section will not see the load and untrusted arbitrary code would be executed. Note this behavior only seems to work on .NET Framework v4, not the older .NET Framework such as v3.5 and v2. From what I can tell in the earlier frameworks, while this check can be bypassed in the same way and the `FlatImageLayout` object created, the runtime passes the assembly to the `LoadLibrary` API later in the loading process where it will fail to load. I didn’t spend much time checking if this was bypassable, as the older .NET Frameworks are no longer installed by default and aren’t even included as optional components in the latest versions of Windows 11. I also didn’t investigate the modern .NET runtimes, v5 and above for similar reasons. ### VirtualBox DLL Loading Hooks Now that we have a potential route to bypassing a process hardening image checker using .NET let’s dig into how it was exploitable in VirtualBox. The previous blog post described how VirtualBox on Windows adds hooks to the DLL loader in order to prevent untrusted images from loading into the process. The important hook for our purposes is the one attached to the `NtCreateSection` system call which is called under the hood by `CreateFileMapping` to create the image section object. The following is the start of the hook function: ``` NTSTATUS supR3HardenedMonitor_NtCreateSection(PHANDLE phSection, ACCESS_MASK fAccess, POBJECT_ATTRIBUTES pObjAttribs, PLARGE_INTEGER pcbSection, ULONG fProtect, ULONG fAttribs, HANDLE hFile) { bool const fExecProt = (fProtect & (PAGE_EXECUTE | PAGE_EXECUTE_READ | PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY | PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE)) != 0; if (hFile != NULL && hFile != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { bool const fImage = RT_BOOL(fAttribs & (SEC_IMAGE | SEC_PROTECTED_IMAGE)); bool const fExecMap = RT_BOOL(fAccess & SECTION_MAP_EXECUTE); if (fImage || fExecMap || fExecProt) { bool fCallRealApi; NTSTATUS rcNt = supR3HardenedScreenImage(hFile, fImage, true /*fIgnoreArch*/, &fAccess, &fProtect, &fCallRealApi, "NtCreateSection", true /*fAvoidWinVerifyTrust*/, NULL /*pfQuiet*/); if (!NT_SUCCESS(rcNt)) return rcNt; if (!fCallRealApi) return STATUS_TRUST_FAILURE; } } NTSTATUS rcNtReal = g_pfnNtCreateSectionReal(phSection, fAccess, pObjAttribs, pcbSection, fProtect, fAttribs, hFile); // ... ``` If the `NtCreateSection` call requests an executable section, such as via the `SEC_IMAGE` flag, then the file is passed to the `supR3HardenedScreenImage` support API which will check if the PE file matches VirtualBox’s loading criteria, only calling the original `NtCreateSection` system call if that succeeds or the file is not being mapped as executable. Importantly the `CreateFileMapping` call in `FlatImageLayout` would not hit the checks as it doesn’t request an image or executable mapping. In order for `CreateFileMapping` to set the `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT` last error, `NtCreateSection` needs to return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT`. We have two options for returning this status code, via the return code of `supR3HardenedScreenImage` or via the call to the original system call. Let’s see if the hardening code can even return this status code? ``` static NTSTATUS supR3HardenedScreenImageCalcStatus(int rc) { if (rc == VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH) return STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT; return STATUS_TRUST_FAILURE; } ``` It turns out that yes, the `supR3HardenedScreenImage` function can return this error code when mapping an internal error code to the status. Specifically if the error code is `VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH` then `supR3HardenedScreenImage` would return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT`. Therefore, what sets `VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH`? This error is set in the PE parser implementation in VirtualBox, specifically in the `rtldrPEOpen` API. This is reachable via `RTLdrOpenWithReader` which is called by the `supHardenedWinVerifyImageByHandle` function which itself is called by `supR3HardenedScreenImage`. To cut a long story short, due to the way the parser is called the `VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH` error is returned if the architecture of the PE file doesn’t match the host architecture and yet the PE file contains executable sections. This turns out to be perfect, when you compile a managed code only .NET assembly as `AnyCPU,` it generates a 32-bit x86 PE file so that it can be run on any system. This is for compatibility, a 64-bit (or ARM64) Windows system can map 32-bit PE files as images, but vice versa is not guaranteed. However, as shown below in the output from the `dumpbin` utility there’s executable code in the file as indicated by the `size of code` field in the optional header. ``` C:\>dumpbin /headers DotNetAssembly.dll Microsoft (R) COFF/PE Dumper Version 14.44.35228.0 Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved. Dump of file DotNetAssembly.dll PE signature found File Type: DLL FILE HEADER VALUES 14C machine (x86) 3 number of sections D62E716A time date stamp 0 file pointer to symbol table 0 number of symbols E0 size of optional header 2022 characteristics Executable Application can handle large (>2GB) addresses DLL OPTIONAL HEADER VALUES 10B magic # (PE32) 48.00 linker version 35CC00 size of code 600 size of initialized data 0 size of uninitialized data ``` Therefore to force the image hardening checks to return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` all we need to do is compile any .NET assembly as `AnyCPU` and it’ll bypass VirtualBox’s image checks without messing with the file format. Crucially, because the .NET assembly DLL has not been modified, it remains a valid assembly which can be loaded by the `FlatImageLayout` class and thus get code execution. The final piece of the puzzle is how to get the assembly DLL loaded into VirtualBox? It’s not sufficient to just cause the DLL to be loaded via `LoadLibrary`, we need .NET to load the file as an assembly file. This is pretty easy to achieve via COM hijacking. We can write a .NET COM registration to the current user’s hive for a class we know a hardened VirtualBox process will load. Then start a VM, that will load the COM object, which loads the .NET runtime which finally loads our untrusted assembly. You can find a full PoC in the issue tracker. There is a small caveat, I haven’t mentioned the WLDP check yet. For VirtualBox this check is unlikely to matter, it will only apply if Windows has a configured code integrity policy which enables the `Dynamic Code Security` or the `UMCI` options. It’s possible a system could have such a policy which also grants VirtualBox’s own binaries to run but it seems unlikely. VirtualBox fixed the issue by never returning `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` from the `supR3HardenedScreenImageCalcStatus` method. They also introduced some new code to make it more difficult to hijack COM objects by using an undocumented global option in COM to disable current user hive lookups. ### Attacking WDAC and Protected Processes If you’ve read this far you might be wondering if the .NET behavior applies to Windows Code Integrity enforcement in general. For example, both Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) and protected processes rely on the in-built code integrity mechanism to block untrusted DLLs from loading, are they vulnerable? Well yes, assuming you can find a way of forcing .NET to use the `FlatImageLayout` option by getting `NtCreateSection` to return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT`. In VirtualBox this condition could be induced due to the behavior of the `NtCreateSection` hook on an unmodified .NET assembly file. For the built-in code integrity case there’s no user-mode hook to abuse, you only have the call to `NtCreateSection`. We need to be able to induce the `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` status code from the system call without a) hitting the code integrity check first and b) the resulting image being invalid for .NET to load. The latter issue seemed to be most problematic, it’s likely that the signature validation would only run once the file was verified to be a valid PE image, but if we modify the file too much then .NET would refuse to load it. We can write a simple test harness to call `NtCreateSection` first with the file, then if that fails with `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` call `Assembly::Load` passing the file path to load and see if that succeeds. From that you could write a fuzzer looking for a suitable modification, or just play with the file format manually. I found that it was almost trivial to create the right conditions. If you clear the `IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE` flag in the COFF File Header’s Characteristics flag field then `NtCreateSection` will fail to load the file as an image section, but it is ignored by .NET when loading the PE file. This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly. This is when the WLDP check becomes important. If an enterprise is deploying a WDAC code integrity policy they have probably enabled `UMCI` or the `Dynamic Code Security` option which blocks this attack. The `Dynamic Code Security` option isn’t enabled by default, and as it disables all dynamic code loading in .NET including the byte array version of `Assembly::Load` it might result in breaking important applications. However, UMCI is one of the main reasons to deploy a WDAC policy as that restricts what user mode code is allowed to run. Still, I decided to try the attack against an installation of Windows 11 S Mode which does enable `UMCI` but doesn’t enable `Dynamic Code Security`. To test it out I needed force .NET to load the assembly file. For Windows 11 S Mode you can run many of the built-in .NET utilities which take assemblies on the command line. For example, the Assembly Registration Tool can be used to load a .NET assembly and call any register and unregister functions defined by the developer. For example, compile the following code as a .NET assembly adding your own code to `UnregisterFunction`: ``` using System; using System.Runtime.InteropServices; public class ComClass { [ComUnregisterFunction] public static void UnregisterFunction(Type t) { //Insert code here. } } ``` Modify the resulting assembly to remove the `IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE` flag. You don’t need to fix up anything else like the image checksum, a hex editor is all you need to change a single bit. Then you can pass the path to the modified assembly DLL to the RegAsm executable from the .NET runtime directory. Note, you should pass the `/unregister` option to run the `UnregisterFunction`, as unregistering doesn’t require administrator privileges. ``` C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\v4.0.30319\regasm.exe c:\path\to\assembly.dll /unregister ``` In theory this should have failed, but it didn’t. The modified assembly was loaded into memory and executed arbitrary code even with UMCI enabled. It turns out that the WLDP check is wrong, at least if only UMCI is enabled. It’s checking that the policy flags are not equal to the `WLDP_LOCKDOWN_CONFIG_CI` flag set, which represents: ``` WLDP_LOCKDOWN_DEFINED_FLAG | WLDP_LOCKDOWN_CONFIG_CI_FLAG | WLDP_LOCKDOWN_UMCIENFORCE_FLAG ``` Unfortunately this is exactly the flag setting returned by `WldpGetLockdownPolicy` on Windows 11 S Mode. Therefore the check passes and loading continues which then bypasses UMCI enforcement. For protected processes on a default installation of Windows the WLDP check doesn’t even come into play. Realistically, .NET should also check for protected status but it doesn’t. It should also be pointed out that you can only exploit Protected Process Light (PPL) processes. The original Protected Process (PP) requires DLLs to have page hashes in their authenticode signature, which the .NET runtime DLLs lack. Thus .NET fails to load, and we can’t reach the vulnerable code. For protected processes you can again abuse COM hijacking again. I found that `WerSecureFault.exe` loads a COM object during runtime, so by hijacking that registration and using the modified .NET DLL I could get arbitrary code as PPL at the TCB level without needing administrator privileges. ## Reporting to Microsoft Once I’d worked out how to abuse this behavior I wondered if it needs to be submitted to Microsoft for fixing. According to the MSRC Security Servicing Criteria any PPL bypass is not in scope. WDAC is a supported security boundary, however to quote the security goal, “Only executable code, including scripts run by enlightened Windows script hosts, that conforms to the device’s policy can run…” This could be interpreted as, if there is a policy that can be enabled to prevent the code from running, then it’s not eligible for fixing. I had assumed that the WLDP check was as designed and it was really the `Dynamic Code Policy` that was disabling this behavior. Therefore I decided not to report it, presenting it at the 2026 44Con conference instead. However, after discussing the issue with some .NET developers they were clear that although enabling `Dynamic Code Policy` blocked the bypass that was by accident and not the intended purpose of the policy. They asked me to submit it to MSRC. Unfortunately by this point, late September 2026, I’d already publicly disclosed therefore it was treated as a zero day, CVE-2026-108398, and was fixed in October 2026, less than a month after reporting. The fix was to correct the WLDP check to the following: ``` DWORD policy = 0; if (EEConfig::EnforceCodeIntegrity() || (SUCCEEDED(WldpGetLockdownPolicy(nullptr, &policy, nullptr)) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_OFF(policy) && WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_ENFORCE(policy)) ) { ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); } ``` The use of `WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_ENFORCE` specifically checks for UMCI being enabled and disabling loading from memory. However this wouldn’t change the behavior in PPL therefore that should still be bypassable. ## Conclusions As with my previous research into VirtualBox’s process hardening on Windows I was able to reuse the bypass to exploit the built in code integrity features of Windows. In this case the .NET code tried to adhere to policy but the developers just made a mistake. Unfortunately the behavior made me assume that it wouldn’t meet MSRC’s security servicing criteria and so the vulnerability wasn’t initially reported. While the criteria are useful, in cases like this where the expected behavior is unclear it can mean a real issue might not get reported. I’d like to thank the .NET team for getting a fix out so quickly.
items.summary_html:
Back in 2017 I did some research into Oracle VirtualBox on Windows. Specifically I focussed on their mechanism to protect their VM processes from the user on the host. The protection was to gate who could open the kernel driver, which might allow for privilege escalation due to the way it was designed. At the time I found 3 ways of bypassing the protection, with an additional issue in COM’s runtime I reported in 2020. These issues were all written up in this post.

Fast forward to 2026 and I decided to look at VirtualBox again to see if much had changed. This time I found 3 new bypasses for protected processes, with an additional bug which was a broken fix for the 2020 bypass breaking due to changes in Windows. In this blog post I want to focus on one specific issue CVE-2026-87268 which abused a feature of the .NET Framework which, when combined with the implementation of the DLL loader hooks implemented by VirtualBox, permitted a bypass of the checks and allowed me to load arbitrary code into the protected process. Let’s dig into the root cause of the issue in .NET first, before moving on to exploitation in VirtualBox.

### .NET Assembly Loading

The .NET Framework is interesting when it comes to bypassing process hardening as it supports loading assemblies from a memory buffer as long as you stick to only using managed code. This is obviously useful if the hardened process is maintained through verifying what DLLs can or cannot be loaded as it bypasses the traditional image mapping process. As the .NET runtime implementation is Microsoft signed, it’s usually permitted to load by any such checks.

The canonical way to load from a memory buffer is to use the Assembly::Load static method which accepts a byte array. This does require you to run some .NET code first, or find a confused deputy to do the work for you. I used this API method to bypass VirtualBox process hardening back in 2017, I was able to get to the API through the JScript script engine, culminating in me releasing the generic DotNetToJScript tool.

I’d always assumed this was the limit of bootstrapping arbitrary .NET from a memory buffer. If you tried to load a .NET assembly from a file it’d map it as an image section which would hit any DLL hardening checks and block an unsigned and untrusted binary from loading. However, in a “Doh” moment I realized I’d never verified this behavior to be true, thus I decided to take a look.

The most important function to mapping a .NET assembly into memory seems to be `PEImageLayout::Map`, which is roughly the following in the version 4 of CLR.DLL which implements the runtime:

```
PEImageLayout *PEImageLayout::Map(HANDLE file) { PEImageLayout* image = new MappedImageLayout(file); if (!image->Image) { image = new FlatImageLayout(file); } if (image->Image) { if (!PEDecoder::CheckFormat(image->Image)) ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); } return image; }
```

What is interesting is this code creates a `MappedImageLayout` object based on the file. If that fails it’ll fall back to using a different object, `FlatImageLayout`. The names kind of give away what they’re doing, but just to be sure let’s look at the implementations of the constructors:

```
void MappedImageLayout::MappedImageLayout(HANDLE file) { HANDLE mapping = CreateFileMapping(file, nullptr, SEC_IMAGE | PAGE_READONLY); if (mapping) { this->Image = CLRMapViewOfFileEx(mapping); } else { if (GetLastError() != ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT) ThrowLastError(); } DWORD policy = 0; if (EEConfig::EnforceCodeIntegrity() || (SUCCEEDED(WldpGetLockdownPolicy(nullptr, &policy, nullptr)) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_OFF(policy) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_CONFIG_CI(policy)) ) { ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); } // ... }
```

The constructor for `MappedImageLayout` uses the CreateFileMapping API to convert the file handle into a section object. The code passes the `SEC_IMAGE` flag which instructs the kernel to assume the file is a PE executable and build an image section object including mapping in executable memory pages. Any protections which rely on verifying an image’s signature or location can be notified and take appropriate action. However if the `CreateFileMapping` call fails the code checks if the last error was not `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT` and throws ending the load entirely.

An additional check is made here to check if “Code Integrity” is enforced through the Windows Lockdown Policy (WLDP) APIs. This checks for the “Dynamic Code Security” code integrity policy being enabled or if a User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI) policy is enforced. If it is then an error is thrown ending the loading process. We’ll come back to this check when it becomes relevant.

Assuming the mapping fails with the `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT` error, then the loading process continues, creating a `FlatImageLayout` object instead:

```
void FlatImageLayout::FlatImageLayout(HANDLE file) { HANDLE mapping = CreateFileMapping(file, nullptr, PAGE_READONLY); if (mapping) { this->Image = CLRMapViewOfFileEx(mapping); } else { ThrowLastError(); } // ... }
```

This constructor is simpler, it just calls `CreateFileMapping` without the `SEC_IMAGE` flag. Therefore the file is mapped into memory as a data only section. There’s no executable pages, but that doesn’t matter for .NET. The final check, back in the first code snippet verifies that the PE file is valid with a call to `PEDecoder::CheckFormat`, throwing if it’s not valid.

The take away from this is if we can get .NET to load a valid assembly file, but cause the first call to `CreateFileMapping` to fail with the `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT` error we can get it to execute the file from memory. Any protection code which is expecting to check the loaded image section will not see the load and untrusted arbitrary code would be executed.

Note this behavior only seems to work on .NET Framework v4, not the older .NET Framework such as v3.5 and v2. From what I can tell in the earlier frameworks, while this check can be bypassed in the same way and the `FlatImageLayout` object created, the runtime passes the assembly to the `LoadLibrary` API later in the loading process where it will fail to load. I didn’t spend much time checking if this was bypassable, as the older .NET Frameworks are no longer installed by default and aren’t even included as optional components in the latest versions of Windows 11. I also didn’t investigate the modern .NET runtimes, v5 and above for similar reasons.

### VirtualBox DLL Loading Hooks

Now that we have a potential route to bypassing a process hardening image checker using .NET let’s dig into how it was exploitable in VirtualBox. The previous blog post described how VirtualBox on Windows adds hooks to the DLL loader in order to prevent untrusted images from loading into the process. The important hook for our purposes is the one attached to the `NtCreateSection` system call which is called under the hood by `CreateFileMapping` to create the image section object. The following is the start of the hook function:

```
NTSTATUS supR3HardenedMonitor_NtCreateSection(PHANDLE phSection, ACCESS_MASK fAccess, POBJECT_ATTRIBUTES pObjAttribs, PLARGE_INTEGER pcbSection, ULONG fProtect, ULONG fAttribs, HANDLE hFile) { bool const fExecProt = (fProtect & (PAGE_EXECUTE | PAGE_EXECUTE_READ | PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY | PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE)) != 0; if (hFile != NULL && hFile != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { bool const fImage = RT_BOOL(fAttribs & (SEC_IMAGE | SEC_PROTECTED_IMAGE)); bool const fExecMap = RT_BOOL(fAccess & SECTION_MAP_EXECUTE); if (fImage || fExecMap || fExecProt) { bool fCallRealApi; NTSTATUS rcNt = supR3HardenedScreenImage(hFile, fImage, true /*fIgnoreArch*/, &fAccess, &fProtect, &fCallRealApi, "NtCreateSection", true /*fAvoidWinVerifyTrust*/, NULL /*pfQuiet*/); if (!NT_SUCCESS(rcNt)) return rcNt; if (!fCallRealApi) return STATUS_TRUST_FAILURE; } } NTSTATUS rcNtReal = g_pfnNtCreateSectionReal(phSection, fAccess, pObjAttribs, pcbSection, fProtect, fAttribs, hFile); // ...
```

If the `NtCreateSection` call requests an executable section, such as via the `SEC_IMAGE` flag, then the file is passed to the `supR3HardenedScreenImage` support API which will check if the PE file matches VirtualBox’s loading criteria, only calling the original `NtCreateSection` system call if that succeeds or the file is not being mapped as executable. Importantly the `CreateFileMapping` call in `FlatImageLayout` would not hit the checks as it doesn’t request an image or executable mapping.

In order for `CreateFileMapping` to set the `ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT` last error, `NtCreateSection` needs to return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT`. We have two options for returning this status code, via the return code of `supR3HardenedScreenImage` or via the call to the original system call. Let’s see if the hardening code can even return this status code?

```
static NTSTATUS supR3HardenedScreenImageCalcStatus(int rc) { if (rc == VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH) return STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT; return STATUS_TRUST_FAILURE; }
```

It turns out that yes, the `supR3HardenedScreenImage` function can return this error code when mapping an internal error code to the status. Specifically if the error code is `VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH` then `supR3HardenedScreenImage` would return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT`. Therefore, what sets `VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH`?

This error is set in the PE parser implementation in VirtualBox, specifically in the `rtldrPEOpen` API. This is reachable via `RTLdrOpenWithReader` which is called by the `supHardenedWinVerifyImageByHandle` function which itself is called by `supR3HardenedScreenImage`.

To cut a long story short, due to the way the parser is called the `VERR_LDR_ARCH_MISMATCH` error is returned if the architecture of the PE file doesn’t match the host architecture and yet the PE file contains executable sections. This turns out to be perfect, when you compile a managed code only .NET assembly as `AnyCPU,` it generates a 32-bit x86 PE file so that it can be run on any system. This is for compatibility, a 64-bit (or ARM64) Windows system can map 32-bit PE files as images, but vice versa is not guaranteed. However, as shown below in the output from the `dumpbin` utility there’s executable code in the file as indicated by the `size of code` field in the optional header.

```
C:\>dumpbin /headers DotNetAssembly.dll Microsoft (R) COFF/PE Dumper Version 14.44.35228.0 Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved. Dump of file DotNetAssembly.dll PE signature found File Type: DLL FILE HEADER VALUES 14C machine (x86) 3 number of sections D62E716A time date stamp 0 file pointer to symbol table 0 number of symbols E0 size of optional header 2022 characteristics Executable Application can handle large (>2GB) addresses DLL OPTIONAL HEADER VALUES 10B magic # (PE32) 48.00 linker version 35CC00 size of code 600 size of initialized data 0 size of uninitialized data
```

Therefore to force the image hardening checks to return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` all we need to do is compile any .NET assembly as `AnyCPU` and it’ll bypass VirtualBox’s image checks without messing with the file format. Crucially, because the .NET assembly DLL has not been modified, it remains a valid assembly which can be loaded by the `FlatImageLayout` class and thus get code execution.

The final piece of the puzzle is how to get the assembly DLL loaded into VirtualBox? It’s not sufficient to just cause the DLL to be loaded via `LoadLibrary`, we need .NET to load the file as an assembly file. This is pretty easy to achieve via COM hijacking. We can write a .NET COM registration to the current user’s hive for a class we know a hardened VirtualBox process will load. Then start a VM, that will load the COM object, which loads the .NET runtime which finally loads our untrusted assembly. You can find a full PoC in the issue tracker.

There is a small caveat, I haven’t mentioned the WLDP check yet. For VirtualBox this check is unlikely to matter, it will only apply if Windows has a configured code integrity policy which enables the `Dynamic Code Security` or the `UMCI` options. It’s possible a system could have such a policy which also grants VirtualBox’s own binaries to run but it seems unlikely.

VirtualBox fixed the issue by never returning `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` from the `supR3HardenedScreenImageCalcStatus` method. They also introduced some new code to make it more difficult to hijack COM objects by using an undocumented global option in COM to disable current user hive lookups.

### Attacking WDAC and Protected Processes

If you’ve read this far you might be wondering if the .NET behavior applies to Windows Code Integrity enforcement in general. For example, both Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) and protected processes rely on the in-built code integrity mechanism to block untrusted DLLs from loading, are they vulnerable?

Well yes, assuming you can find a way of forcing .NET to use the `FlatImageLayout` option by getting `NtCreateSection` to return `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT`. In VirtualBox this condition could be induced due to the behavior of the `NtCreateSection` hook on an unmodified .NET assembly file.

For the built-in code integrity case there’s no user-mode hook to abuse, you only have the call to `NtCreateSection`. We need to be able to induce the `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` status code from the system call without a) hitting the code integrity check first and b) the resulting image being invalid for .NET to load. The latter issue seemed to be most problematic, it’s likely that the signature validation would only run once the file was verified to be a valid PE image, but if we modify the file too much then .NET would refuse to load it.

We can write a simple test harness to call `NtCreateSection` first with the file, then if that fails with `STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT` call `Assembly::Load` passing the file path to load and see if that succeeds. From that you could write a fuzzer looking for a suitable modification, or just play with the file format manually.

I found that it was almost trivial to create the right conditions. If you clear the `IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE` flag in the COFF File Header’s Characteristics flag field then `NtCreateSection` will fail to load the file as an image section, but it is ignored by .NET when loading the PE file. This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly.

This is when the WLDP check becomes important. If an enterprise is deploying a WDAC code integrity policy they have probably enabled `UMCI` or the `Dynamic Code Security` option which blocks this attack. The `Dynamic Code Security` option isn’t enabled by default, and as it disables all dynamic code loading in .NET including the byte array version of `Assembly::Load` it might result in breaking important applications.

However, UMCI is one of the main reasons to deploy a WDAC policy as that restricts what user mode code is allowed to run. Still, I decided to try the attack against an installation of Windows 11 S Mode which does enable `UMCI` but doesn’t enable `Dynamic Code Security`.

To test it out I needed force .NET to load the assembly file. For Windows 11 S Mode you can run many of the built-in .NET utilities which take assemblies on the command line. For example, the Assembly Registration Tool can be used to load a .NET assembly and call any register and unregister functions defined by the developer. For example, compile the following code as a .NET assembly adding your own code to `UnregisterFunction`:

```
using System; using System.Runtime.InteropServices; public class ComClass { [ComUnregisterFunction] public static void UnregisterFunction(Type t) { //Insert code here. } }
```

Modify the resulting assembly to remove the `IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE` flag. You don’t need to fix up anything else like the image checksum, a hex editor is all you need to change a single bit. Then you can pass the path to the modified assembly DLL to the RegAsm executable from the .NET runtime directory. Note, you should pass the `/unregister` option to run the `UnregisterFunction`, as unregistering doesn’t require administrator privileges.

```
C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\v4.0.30319\regasm.exe c:\path\to\assembly.dll /unregister
```

In theory this should have failed, but it didn’t. The modified assembly was loaded into memory and executed arbitrary code even with UMCI enabled. It turns out that the WLDP check is wrong, at least if only UMCI is enabled. It’s checking that the policy flags are not equal to the `WLDP_LOCKDOWN_CONFIG_CI` flag set, which represents:

```
WLDP_LOCKDOWN_DEFINED_FLAG | WLDP_LOCKDOWN_CONFIG_CI_FLAG | WLDP_LOCKDOWN_UMCIENFORCE_FLAG
```

Unfortunately this is exactly the flag setting returned by `WldpGetLockdownPolicy` on Windows 11 S Mode. Therefore the check passes and loading continues which then bypasses UMCI enforcement.

For protected processes on a default installation of Windows the WLDP check doesn’t even come into play. Realistically, .NET should also check for protected status but it doesn’t. It should also be pointed out that you can only exploit Protected Process Light (PPL) processes. The original Protected Process (PP) requires DLLs to have page hashes in their authenticode signature, which the .NET runtime DLLs lack. Thus .NET fails to load, and we can’t reach the vulnerable code.

For protected processes you can again abuse COM hijacking again. I found that `WerSecureFault.exe` loads a COM object during runtime, so by hijacking that registration and using the modified .NET DLL I could get arbitrary code as PPL at the TCB level without needing administrator privileges.

## Reporting to Microsoft

Once I’d worked out how to abuse this behavior I wondered if it needs to be submitted to Microsoft for fixing. According to the MSRC Security Servicing Criteria any PPL bypass is not in scope. WDAC is a supported security boundary, however to quote the security goal, “Only executable code, including scripts run by enlightened Windows script hosts, that conforms to the device’s policy can run…” This could be interpreted as, if there is a policy that can be enabled to prevent the code from running, then it’s not eligible for fixing.

I had assumed that the WLDP check was as designed and it was really the `Dynamic Code Policy` that was disabling this behavior. Therefore I decided not to report it, presenting it at the 2026 44Con conference instead.

However, after discussing the issue with some .NET developers they were clear that although enabling `Dynamic Code Policy` blocked the bypass that was by accident and not the intended purpose of the policy. They asked me to submit it to MSRC. Unfortunately by this point, late September 2026, I’d already publicly disclosed therefore it was treated as a zero day, CVE-2026-108398, and was fixed in October 2026, less than a month after reporting.

The fix was to correct the WLDP check to the following:

```
DWORD policy = 0; if (EEConfig::EnforceCodeIntegrity() || (SUCCEEDED(WldpGetLockdownPolicy(nullptr, &policy, nullptr)) && !WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_OFF(policy) && WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_ENFORCE(policy)) ) { ThrowWin32(ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT); }
```

The use of `WLDP_LOCKDOWN_IS_ENFORCE` specifically checks for UMCI being enabled and disabling loading from memory. However this wouldn’t change the behavior in PPL therefore that should still be bypassable.

## Conclusions

As with my previous research into VirtualBox’s process hardening on Windows I was able to reuse the bypass to exploit the built in code integrity features of Windows. In this case the .NET code tried to adhere to policy but the developers just made a mistake.

Unfortunately the behavior made me assume that it wouldn’t meet MSRC’s security servicing criteria and so the vulnerability wasn’t initially reported. While the criteria are useful, in cases like this where the expected behavior is unclear it can mean a real issue might not get reported. I’d like to thank the .NET team for getting a fix out so quickly.

items.title: BADBOX 3.0 Exposed: Massive Botnet Hides Ad Fraud Inside Android TV Boxes
items.summary: BADBOX 3.0 returns with 40 billion daily ad requests, turning infected TV boxes into fraud machines The BADBOX botnet is back, and its latest version has reached a scale that makes previous ad fraud operations look relatively small. Researchers from HUMAN’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research team have uncovered BADBOX 3.0, a large-scale operation that uses infected Android-based TV boxes and other low-cost consumer devices to generate billions of fraudulent advertising requests every day. “At its height, BADBOX 3.0 accounted for roughly 40 billion bid requests a day and more than 4% of all CTV traffic observed by the Human Defense Platform. BADBOX 3.0’s volume was more than three times the volume of the previous record holder , VASTFLUX, and represents a larger peak than the last five years’ worth of published Satori investigations combined .” reads the report published by Human. “BADBOX 3.0 runs primarily on low-cost consumer devices infected with new backdoors that deliver fraud modules, including some that HUMAN researchers recognized from BADBOX and BADBOX 2.0 .” According to the investigation, the operation peaked at around 40 billion bid requests per day, accounting for more than 4% of all connected TV (CTV) traffic observed by HUMAN’s Defense Platform. That’s more than three times the volume attributed to VASTFLUX , the previous record holder. The latest findings show that the operators haven’t simply rebuilt the previous botnet. They’ve expanded its capabilities by combining advertising fraud with the abuse of residential proxy networks, using the same compromised devices for both activities. “The investigation began with a backdoor packaged as a system application with two hardcoded endpoints.” continues the report. “One endpoint retrieves the list of modules to load in the background, and the second handles logging.” BADBOX 3.0 primarily targets inexpensive, off-brand Android devices, including TV boxes, smartphones and tablets running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP). Some of these devices reportedly arrive with backdoors already installed, allowing attackers to gain privileged access and install additional malicious components. The advertising fraud works by running video ads in hidden windows. The infected device plays the ads in the background, while the malware generates advertising requests that impersonate legitimate connected TV applications. Advertisers and advertising platforms therefore receive what appears to be genuine traffic from popular streaming services, even though the applications being impersonated aren’t actually running on the infected devices. “Modules delivered through BADBOX 3.0 mimic video ad software development kits (SDKs) and render the ads in a hidden window, so the ad plays on the device while the screen shows nothing unusual.” HUMAN researchers report. “The resulting bid requests present themselves as coming from well-known, legitimate CTV apps that the threat actors impersonated to route their traffic. “ The investigation also uncovered another revenue stream. The malware silently enrolls infected devices in residential proxy networks, turning their owners’ internet connections into infrastructure that third parties can rent and use. Researchers identified 11 such networks, including ten commercially available services and PXYEDGE, a network allegedly operated by the same threat actors behind the BADBOX campaigns. “One of those networks is PXYEDGE, the rebranded successor to the IpMoYu network exposed in BADBOX 2.0.” the report states. “Not all of the operation’s ad fraud requires an infected device: HUMAN also observed spoofed server-side ad insertion (SSAI) traffic monetized through many of the same supply paths.” The device owner unknowingly provides the bandwidth and residential IP address, while someone else monetizes that access. This creates a problem that extends beyond advertising fraud. Residential proxies can help criminals conceal the origin of their activities, making it harder to identify attacks involving account takeovers, fake account creation, payment card fraud and other forms of abuse. The report also establishes a connection between PXYEDGE and IpMoYu, the residential proxy network previously exposed during the BADBOX 2.0 investigation. Researchers found overlapping infrastructure, proxy modules and task servers, concluding that PXYEDGE is likely IpMoYu operating under a different name. They also observed approximately 340,000 unique connections across monitored services, while the network advertised around 200,000 available nodes. “The eleventh network is PXYEDGE , operated by the threat actors themselves and described below.” Human states. “Enrolling a device in these networks turns the owner’s home internet connection into a commodity without their knowledge or consent. The device owner pays for the bandwidth, and someone else sells access to the address. “ Another important finding concerns the infrastructure behind the operation. Satori researchers linked the BADBOX 3.0 malware catalog to TXCZ, a Chinese electronics manufacturer, through several independent technical connections. These include command-and-control infrastructure, manufacturer-owned domains, preinstalled software, device-specific checks embedded in the malware and public code repositories used to distribute malicious modules. Researchers also identified a repository account incorporating TXCZ’s name and linked its maintainer to the threat activity. These findings establish several connections between the malware infrastructure and the manufacturer. They don’t, by themselves, establish the extent of the company’s knowledge or involvement in the criminal operation. The operators have also taken steps to make the botnet harder to disrupt. Instead of relying on a single download location, they distribute malicious modules through public code repositories and multiple backup hosting services. Some payloads are mirrored through an open-source content delivery network, while a self-hosted GitHub proxy helps devices retrieve files even when access to the original repositories is blocked. This approach also gives researchers visibility into the malware’s development. By examining repository histories, Satori identified an actively maintained catalog containing hundreds of module versions, including components associated with earlier BADBOX campaigns and the vo1d malware family. BADBOX has survived previous disruption efforts. Researchers first discovered the malware in 2023, when they found low-cost Android devices with a backdoor already installed in their firmware. In 2025, they uncovered BADBOX 2.0, a much larger operation that had infected more than 10 million devices across 222 countries and territories. Google, HUMAN, Trend Micro, Shadowserver and other partners then worked together to disrupt it. However, as BleepingComputer reports, the operators have returned with a new version. HUMAN also joined a separate operation led by Google to disrupt XCPE, a related but different malware campaign. Researchers found more than one million infected devices in over 200 countries and territories. The operation also helped identify and take down several command-and-control domains used by BADBOX 3.0. The researchers stress that disrupting the infrastructure doesn’t necessarily eliminate the threat. Previous investigations showed that the operators could rebuild their capabilities by moving to new servers, changing distribution methods and adapting their malware. For consumers, the advice remains straightforward: buy devices from reputable manufacturers, check that Android devices are Play Protect certified, and install applications only through official marketplaces. Cheap, uncertified Android TV boxes deserve particular scrutiny, especially when their software and manufacturer cannot be independently verified. The most important lesson from BADBOX 3.0 is that a consumer device can become part of a criminal operation without its owner noticing anything unusual. It can generate fraudulent advertising revenue, provide access to a residential internet connection and help conceal other malicious activities. The problem isn’t limited to the money lost by advertisers. It’s also about consumers unknowingly providing the infrastructure criminals need to operate. “Each chapter of this research has ended with a version of the same observation: disrupting an operation and dismantling the conditions that produced it are different achievements.” the report concludes. “BADBOX 3.0 shows what that intact supply chain produces. The capability now lives in public code repositories, mirrored across hosting platforms, a mainstream CDN, and a proxy built to slip past network blocks, with fallback locations written into every module record. Its proxy network survived exposure by changing its name.
